method: Live console, read-only. Actions menu opened against a stopped instance and a running instance; every item's aria-disabled recorded. Nothing was invoked.
why_this_matters: Column inventories are the easy thing to measure and the wrong thing to optimise. What separates this mock from the console is interaction grammar: what a selection enables, what state a command requires, and what an action leaves behind. The state-dependence below is the part that makes a task non-trivial — 'change the instance type' is a three-step task because the console refuses it while the instance runs.

nothing_selected.Actions: enabled — the trigger is never disabled; individual items are

one_selected.heading: Instances (1/29) — the heading carries selected/total, not just total
one_selected.Connect: enabled when the instance is running

actions_menu.structure: nested — six submenus plus a top-level group, separated by dividers

state_dependent_enablement.note: Derived by diffing the menu against a stopped instance and a running instance in the same account.

disabled_in_both_states.reason: Each depends on a property the sampled instances lack — hibernation not enabled at launch, not a SQL Server or Windows AMI, ENA Express unsupported on the instance type. These are capability-gated rather than state-gated, and a faithful mock should gate them on the same properties.

task_design_implication: Because the console refuses Change instance type while an instance runs, resizing is inherently multi-step: stop, wait for the state transition, change, start. A mock that lets the type be changed at any time erases that structure and with it the training signal.
